binding_limiters: The single bounded research pass tested eight structurally varied candidates with 6-12 sources each; all eight were stopped because direct incumbents or native systems already cover the wedge and no candidate demonstrated a separately paid, founder-accessible control point with validated data or partner rights, conservative contribution economics, repeatable low-touch distribution, and a plausible bottom-up founder-net-worth path.

correction.reason: The official score is N/A because this run produced zero evaluations. N/A is not a score of zero, and the prior no_qualifier label was invalid because no candidate completed native holdout scoring.

no_finalist_reason: The single bounded research pass tested eight candidates with 6-12 sources each, but it stopped before every mandatory working evaluation, development attempt, redesign decision, finalist freeze, and native holdout. The research artifacts remain useful diagnostic evidence, but this run cannot support a qualification decision.

portfolio_decision.reason: High-frequency non-exempt demand, contractor payment, collector margin, and differentiation from incumbents were unproven.
A 15% dispatch margin yielded about PLN 57 per building per year, insufficient for coordination, quality assurance, and liability.
Exact audits were already free or contingency-priced, while profitable sites required unusually high recoverable leakage.
PSE's WOZE system and existing vendors covered claims, and incremental under-recovery was not demonstrated.
KSeF did not reliably show payment status, while ERP dunning, collections, and factoring already covered the workflow.
Processor-native tools and Chargeflow already automated the workflow, and typical dispute values and win rates weakened the economics.
Employer-clinic contracts restricted open routing, while medical networks already bundled the service.
Existing operators provided the same around-the-clock service; backend rights, field operations, and part-time founder feasibility failed.

contrary_evidence: EVia Charge already advertises a vendor-neutral OCPP 1.6/2.0 platform with 24/7 monitoring, billing, fault detection, technical support, and on-site service in Warsaw.
GreenWay sells continuous monitoring, settlement, service, reporting, and 24/7 operations as one established CEE bundle.
ABB can bundle monitoring, remote updates, certified repair, field response, warranty, and parts and reports 60% remote resolution on its connected platform.
E-Flux prices alerts and remote reset/unlock at only EUR 5.50 per AC socket/month and EUR 10.40 per DC socket/month, compressing the software-only value.
EIPA status fields are too shallow to assign fault ownership, and UDT disclaims timeliness of operator-provided data.
Public reliability evidence shows failures but does not prove Polish willingness to pay an additional independent operator.
The operational moat depends on certified technicians, parts, travel, on-call coverage, and regulated return-to-service work rather than scalable software alone.
risks: No separate budget: buyers may treat monitoring and uptime as already included in CPO, CPMS, installer, warranty, or OEM contracts.
No control rights: the desk may see an outage but be unable to issue safe remote commands, access logs, change firmware, or authorize repair.
Measurement liability: a binary public status can disagree with actual charge success, creating false accusations and poor prospecting.
Warranty and cybersecurity liability from third-party access or intervention.
Direct substitution by GreenWay, EVia, OEM service, and low-cost multi-brand CPMS products.
24/7 customer expectation conflicts with part-time founder availability and forces early fixed operating cost.
Field coordination scales with incidents, geography, parts, and people; software does not remove those constraints.
UDT and certified-repair requirements can delay return to service and create documentation obligations.
Customer concentration is likely because each fleet sale carries many connectors, weakening private-company valuation.
The founder-wealth target requires thousands of connectors and expansion or displacement before any route to PLN 5 million becomes credible.

uncertainties: Addressable count of 20-500-connector Polish and CEE fleets after excluding mobility-only entities, single-site operators, large incumbents, and assets already covered by comprehensive contracts.
Separate annual budget and economic buyer for reliability operations.
Backend, remote-command, log, firmware, payment-data, warranty, and repair rights by fleet and manufacturer.
Polish mixed-brand fault mix, incident rate, remote-close rate, one-visit-close rate, repeat-fault rate, and false-public-status rate.
Technician density, on-call premiums, travel time, parts lead time, UDT delay, and field contribution margin.
Commercial reuse and outreach rights for EIPA-derived fleet and outage reports and contractual rights for non-public operational data.
Paid pilot conversion, CAC, sales cycle, onboarding cost, retention, and service-credit exposure.
Whether the founder can validate under a business-hours SLA when competitors promise 24/7 support.

Low inspection ticket sizes make travel, rework, support and insurance allocation larger than the dispatch margin.
The founder may need an operations hire before revenue supports one, breaking the part-time and capital constraints.

Whether c-KOB supports any API or only role-based/manual work for this use case.
Whether contracts permit de-identified defect and performance benchmarks to be retained and reused.
Whether direct account acquisition can scale from one evidenced 415-object buyer to 70 100-building managers.
